messages.author: 54788cf3a8eb8916
messages.subject: Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
parts:
Hi,
I have attempted to implement (in Rstan) the model discussed in chapter 13 of the Stan manual v2.2.

library(rstan)
lpmodel <- '
  data {
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
    int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
    real y[N];      // observations
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta; // mixing proportions
    real mu[K];       // locations of mixture components
    real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma[K]; // scales of mixture components
  }
  model {
    real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities
    for (k in 1:K) {
      mu[k] ~ normal(0,10);
    }
    for (n in 1:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
        ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
      }
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }'
# prepare the data - a mixture of Normal(-1,2), Normal (3,1)
# with proportion theta = (0.3, 0.7) respectively
Ndata <- 500 # total number of data points
aprop <- 0.3
bprop <- 1 - aprop
aN <- round(Ndata * aprop)
bN <- Ndata - aN
A <- rnorm(aN, -1, 2)
B <- rnorm(bN, 3, 1)
data <- c(A, B)
library(ggplot2) # in case it isn't mentioned earlier
qplot(data, geom='histogram')
# now convert this into Stan friendly format
stan_data <- list(K=2, N=Ndata, y=data)

set_cppo('fast')
fit <- stan(model_code=lpmodel, data=stan_data, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
print(fit)
plot(fit)
traceplot(fit)

As can be seen in the attached knitr'd pdf file, the chains appear to converge to two different modes (am I imagining things?).  The parameters do appear to be recovered - but not in a simple fashion as the chains cannot be merged or can they?

What happens next in the analysis? How are these multiple modes normally handled?

In my analysis I expect to have a mixture of about 20 reasonably distinct Gaussians - can I expect to get 20 modes? 

Your thoughts on this will be appreciated.
 
Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
Trinity College,
Dublin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
parts:
Are the two distinct modes just swapping indices? We talk
about that in the manual. See also the section on problematic
models.

Inferences that don't depend on indexe identifiers are fine
with multiple chains.

It's just that there's no way to use the convergence diagnostics
because each chain doesn't mix across modes.

Unfortunately, the problem is worse than multiplicative.
With 20 indices you get 20! modes.

What many people tend to do in practice is just use inference
from a single long-running chain. But you may want to
run multiple chains just to make sure they're getting into
the same neighborhood on log probbability (lp__ "parameter"
in the output).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
parts:
I discuss this problem a bit in the mixture modeling chapter
and in the problematic posteriors chapter.

The biggest problem is that forcing mu[0] < mu[1], you can still swap
indices if the posterior means of the two mixture components are near each
other (on their scales).

Also, forcing this relationship means that you can't do inference
about how well separated the means are, for instance, Pr[mu[0] < mu[1]] = 1.
I'm pretty sure it will also affect the correlation of mu[0] and mu[1] in the
posterior. Basically, it's not just the same model with identity resolved.

- Bob
